On the [section overview](posterior-computation.qmd#from-a-weighted-grid-to-an-expectation),
we calculated a posterior mean in two ways. We first multiplied each possible
value by its posterior probability and added the products. We then imagined a
collection of draws in which each value appeared in proportion to that
probability and took their ordinary mean. The calculations agreed because draw
frequency took the place of posterior weight.

**[Monte Carlo integration](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html)**
generalizes that second calculation. *Monte
Carlo* means that we use random draws; *integration* names the operation we
want those draws to approximate. The method will let us estimate posterior
means, probabilities, variances, and many other summaries with the same basic
recipe.

The remaining question is how accurate a finite draw average is. If we ask
the computer for another collection of random draws, we will generally get a
slightly different answer. We will treat the draw average as an
[estimator](properties-of-estimators.qmd#estimators-are-random-variables) and
use its [standard error](standard-errors.qmd) to describe this repeated-run
variation. This standard error concerns the computation. It should remain
separate from the spread of the posterior distribution we are approximating.

We will first derive the draw average from a weighted sum. We will then apply
the calculation to the passage-level Student-$t$ model and use a running
estimate to see its numerical variation. The final step separates three
sources of approximation introduced by the grid demonstration.

## From a weighted sum to a draw average

Suppose we can draw independently from the posterior. For a concrete case,
let $g(\mu,\lambda)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$, where
$\lambda=\log\sigma$. Each draw then produces a zero or a one:

$$
g(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})
=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }\mu^{(s)}>0,\\
0 & \text{if }\mu^{(s)}\leq 0.
\end{cases}
$$

The average of these zeros and ones is simply the proportion of posterior
draws for which $\mu$ is positive. Thus, if 7,432 of 10,000 draws have
$\mu^{(s)}>0$, our Monte Carlo estimate is $7{,}432/10{,}000=.7432$. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

Now write the same idea for a general function $g$. Let
$f(\mu,\lambda\mid\mathbf y)$ denote the joint posterior density in the two
coordinates $\mu$ and $\lambda=\log\sigma$. The posterior expectation is

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\mu,\lambda)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
g(\mu,\lambda)f(\mu,\lambda\mid\mathbf y)
\,\mathrm d\lambda\,\mathrm d\mu.
$$

Independent target draws give the estimator

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)}).
$$

Why should the average approach the integral? Imagine dividing the posterior
into many small regions. A region containing five percent of the posterior
probability will produce about five percent of a large collection of draws.
Its contribution to the draw average therefore approaches its contribution to
the posterior-weighted integral. This is the same frequency-for-weight
substitution we used in the four-row example.

Because the $g(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})$ values are independent with variance
$\operatorname{Var}[g(\mu,\lambda)\mid\mathbf y]$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat I_S\mid\mathbf y]
=
\frac{1}{S^2}
\sum_{s=1}^S
\operatorname{Var}[g(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})\mid\mathbf y]
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}[g(\mu,\lambda)\mid\mathbf y]}{S}.
$$

Taking the square root yields the MCSE formula used below.

Setting $g(\mu,\lambda)=\mu$ estimates the posterior mean of the passage
location. Setting $g(\mu,\lambda)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$ estimates its
directional probability, while $g(\mu,\lambda)=\exp(\mu)$ gives a central
geometric-scale noun-to-verb ratio.

## Drawing from the posterior grid

The code below reconstructs the passage-level Student-t model from the 55 passage summaries, normalizes its $321\times321$ reference grid, and samples 20,000 grid cells with their posterior weights.

Three approximations must be separated. First, truncation error arises if the finite grid omits posterior mass. Second, discretization error arises because a continuous density is represented by grid cells. Third, Monte Carlo error arises because only $S$ cells are sampled from the normalized grid. The equal spacings make every cell area identical, so that area cancels when `grid$weight` is normalized. Approximating the absolute evidence, rather than relative weights, would require multiplying by the cell area.

```{r}
#| label: provo-grid-monte-carlo
provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
N <- length(y)
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)

log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
  maximum <- max(x)
  maximum + log(sum(exp(x - maximum)))
}

log_posterior_pair <- function(parameter_pair) {
  mu <- parameter_pair[1]
  sigma <- exp(parameter_pair[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + parameter_pair[2]
}

mode_fit <- optim(
  c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
  function(parameter_pair) -log_posterior_pair(parameter_pair),
  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L)
)
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
mu_grid <- seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
               mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L)
log_sigma_grid <- seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                      mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
grid <- expand.grid(mu = mu_grid, log_sigma = log_sigma_grid)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_posterior_pair)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))

set.seed(2026101802)
S <- 20000L
draw_indices <- sample(seq_len(nrow(grid)), S, replace = TRUE,
                       prob = grid$weight)
draws <- grid[draw_indices, ]

quadrature <- c(
  mean_mu = sum(grid$mu * grid$weight),
  probability_mu_positive = sum(grid$weight[grid$mu > 0]),
  mean_exp_mu = sum(exp(grid$mu) * grid$weight)
)
estimate <- c(
  mean(draws$mu), mean(draws$mu > 0), mean(exp(draws$mu))
)
mcse <- c(
  sd(draws$mu) / sqrt(S),
  sqrt(estimate[2] * (1 - estimate[2]) / S),
  sd(exp(draws$mu)) / sqrt(S)
)

stopifnot(N == 55L, abs(sum(grid$weight) - 1) < 1e-12)
data.frame(functional = names(quadrature), quadrature, estimate, mcse)
```

The grid benchmark and Monte Carlo estimates agree to the scale of their Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSEs). For independent draws,

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat I_S)
=
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(g(\mu,\lambda))}{S}}.
$$

For an indicator this becomes

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}
=
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat I_S(1-\widehat I_S)}{S}}.
$$

Multiplying $S$ by four tends to halve MCSE. This square-root rate concerns the approximation, not the posterior spread.

The value $S=20{,}000$ controls numerical precision. It does not enter the
likelihood or prior. The reported MCSEs show what this many draws buys; reducing
the desired numerical tolerance by half would require roughly four times as
many independent draws.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-monte-carlo-running
#| fig-cap: "Running Monte Carlo estimate of the passage-level Student-t model directional probability. The horizontal line is the quadrature reference."
library(ggplot2)
running <- cumsum(draws$mu > 0) / seq_len(S)
display_index <- unique(round(seq(10, S, length.out = 600L)))
running_display <- data.frame(
  draws = display_index,
  estimate = running[display_index]
)

ggplot(running_display, aes(draws, estimate)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = quadrature[2], color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Independent grid draws",
       y = "Estimated posterior probability that mu > 0") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The law of large numbers justifies convergence of the average when the
expectation exists. A central limit theorem motivates MCSE when
$g(\mu,\lambda)$ has finite variance. Neither result says that the
passage-level Student-t model's passage aggregation, likelihood, or
empirically calibrated priors are adequate.

## Two uncertainties

Posterior spread describes model-based uncertainty about the passage-level
Student-t model. Monte Carlo error describes finite numerical approximation.
Increasing $S$ reduces the latter while leaving the collection of passages,
positions, and readers exactly as it was. The additional draws refine a
calculation based on the existing evidence.

## Recap and forward link

1. A posterior expectation is an integral; a draw average estimates that integral.
2. Grid truncation, grid discretization, and finite-draw Monte Carlo error are distinct.
3. MCSE decreases at a square-root rate, while posterior spread changes only with the model or linguistic data.

The [importance-sampling page](importance-sampling.qmd#reweighting-a-proposal) next estimates the same expectations without drawing directly from the target.

## Check your understanding

1. Which function $g$ estimates $\mathbb{P}(\mu>0\mid\mathbf y)$?
2. Why is the estimate an integral approximation?
3. What happens to MCSE when $S$ is quadrupled?
4. Which uncertainty requires additional linguistic observations to change?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Use the indicator $g(\mu,\lambda)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The sample average replaces the posterior integral of $g(\mu,\lambda)$ with an empirical average over draws from that posterior. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Quadrupling $S$ tends to halve MCSE because MCSE decreases at the $1/\sqrt S$ rate. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Posterior uncertainty about the linguistic target changes with additional linguistic observations; more simulation draws change only computational uncertainty. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
$\mu^{(s)}>0$, our Monte Carlo estimate is $7{,}432/10{,}000=.7432$. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->
